title: Hyponatraemia
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Symptom-based severity, hypertonic saline for severe symptoms, volume status, correction-rate limits, osmotic demyelination risk, causes. Candidate sources to verify: European clinical practice guideline on hyponatraemia (ESE/ESICM/ERA); US expert panel recommendations.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) emergency treatment of severe or moderately severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, based on the Society for Endocrinology 2022 emergency guidance and a Royal Devon acute medicine pathway. Chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia and the full cause work-up are outside this protocol. No Saudi national guideline was found.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal ranges are typical adult values, not from the cited guidelines.
Symptoms, signs, precipitants, differentials and pathophysiology are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line.
The Society for Endocrinology document has no page numbers and no printed date; section, figure and recommendation numbers are cited.
The 2022 guidance gives no desmopressin dose; the Royal Devon 5% dextrose rate for over-correction has no stopping rule in the opened text.

Royal Devon specifies 2.7% saline while the Society for Endocrinology specifies 3%; the difference was not reconciled and product availability (Saudi Food and Drug Authority registration) was not checked.
No Saudi national or Saudi Ministry of Health hyponatraemia guideline was found.
The Society for Endocrinology guidance does not state the treatment of moderately severe symptoms in detail; the exact boundary for hypertonic saline in that group needs senior confirmation.

The Royal Hospital for Women procedure is written for women in a hospital in Sydney, is past its review date and its Appendix 1 (bag size, preparation, line type, desmopressin and 5% glucose rates) was not in the opened text; its two stated sodium limits (4–8 versus 8 mmol/24 hours after the first day) also differ. Use it only for the infusion monitoring and the three-infusion limit, and not for bag size or rates.

The 3% saline bag size, central versus peripheral line and the desmopressin dose for over-correction are not stated in any opened source; so they are left out of this protocol; take the 3% saline bag volume from the product label.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Hyponatraemia is a low serum sodium that reflects an excess of water relative to sodium.
keyMechanisms: Causes include diuretics, the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, heart failure, cirrhosis, vomiting or diarrhoea, and excess water intake.
A fall in sodium moves water into brain cells; brain swelling causes headache, vomiting, seizures and coma.
Over-correction can cause osmotic demyelination, so the rate of correction is limited.

symptoms: Nausea without vomiting, headache, confusion (moderately severe).
physicalSigns: Volume status: dry, normal or fluid overloaded; reduced Glasgow Coma Scale; seizure.
redFlags: Cardiorespiratory arrest, seizures or Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 or less.
Severe symptoms with sodium above 130 mmol/L suggest another neurological cause.
precipitants: Thiazide diuretics, antidepressants, carbamazepine, adrenal crisis, water loading, marathon running, ecstasy.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Normal measured osmolality (very high lipids or protein)
Very high glucose; sodium rises as glucose falls
Focal signs with sodium above 130 mmol/L

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Assess symptoms and airway, breathing, circulation and consciousness.
Severe symptoms: give an intravenous bolus of hypertonic saline without waiting for the cause.
Moderately severe symptoms: senior review; hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms and moderately severe cases per the 2022 guidance.
Aim for an initial rise of 5 mmol/L in the first hour.
Do not use vaptans or the Adrogue–Madias formula.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: If no improvement after the first rise, give one more bolus aiming for a further 1 mmol/L rise.
Check sodium at 6 hours, 12 hours and then daily until stable.
Monitor urine output; a rise can signal rapid correction.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Over-correction (more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, or 8 mmol/L per 24 hours after that): stop hypertonic fluid and consult an experienced clinician.
Options for over-correction include hypotonic fluid to limit the rise or re-lower sodium, with or without parenteral desmopressin; the 2022 guidance gives no dose.
Royal Devon uses 5% dextrose at 125 mL/hour if the rise exceeds 10 mmol/24 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition
actions: Admit to a monitored setting with senior supervision.

regimens.dose: 150 mL of 3% sodium chloride (hypertonic saline; ready-made bag, volume drawn as the 150 mL bolus)
regimens.route: IV infusion by infusion pump over 20 minutes, with cardiac monitoring, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, neurological observations and strict fluid balance during the infusion (Royal Hospital for Women procedure)
regimens.frequency: Once; if no improvement after a 5 mmol/L rise give one more bolus aiming for a further 1 mmol/L rise; repeat up to 3 infusions in total in a monitored setting
regimens.duration: Stop at symptom improvement, a 10 mmol/L rise or sodium of 130 mmol/L, whichever is first
adjustments: Severe renal impairment: give with particular caution (sodium retention)
liver disease or cirrhosis: caution (sodium retention)
age 65 and over: start at the low end of the dose range
monitoring: Sodium every 2–4 hours during the infusion (Royal Hospital for Women) and at 6 hours, 12 hours and daily (Society for Endocrinology)
stop at symptom improvement or the target rise
contraindications: give in a monitored setting, not on a general ward

learningObjectives: Grade hyponatraemia by symptoms and biochemistry.
Give a hypertonic bolus safely and recognise over-correction.
pitfalls: Using continuous hypertonic infusion instead of boluses.
Using vaptans or the Adrogue–Madias formula.
Missing over-correction after recovery from adrenal crisis.
keyPoints: Treat severe symptoms with a 150 mL bolus of 3% saline over 20 minutes.
Never exceed 10 mmol/L rise in 24 hours.
